sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.

Unlike typical 2D generation workflows (Chang et al., 2025; Ho et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2025; 2024), code-based 3D generation produces structured, executable content that users can edit, reuse, compose, and inspect. These properties enable scalable, controllable 3D modeling for diverse applications. Recent advances in language models and coding agents further automate this process, allowing users to create complex 3D content through text instructions (Sun et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2026). Despite these advances, shared infrastructure for developing and evaluating 3D coding systems across environments remains limited. Existing resources address complementary aspects of 3D coding: DeepCAD and BlenderLLM provide supervision for CAD construction and Blender scripting (Wu et al., 2021; Du et al., 2024); SceneCraft and VIGA refine generated content using visual feedback (Hu et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2026); and Articraft combines specialized SDK with harness for articulated asset generation (Zhou et al., 2026). However, these resources remain fragmented across tasks and environments. As shown in Table 1, existing datasets primarily focus on static or articulated objects, while harnesses vary in their support for visual assessment and automated corpus construction. To bridge these gaps, we introduce 3DCodeVerse (Figure 1), an open-source foundational framework for learning and scaling 3D coding through large-scale executable code corpus and 3D code generation harness. We first build 3DCodeVerse-2M, unified corpus of executable 3D programs spanning static objects, articulated assets, scenes, and graphics. Rather than simply aggregating existing datasets, we systematically convert heterogeneous 3D representations into reusable source code and remove dependencies on specialized or unavailable libraries. For example, we translate DeepCAD construction sequences into CadQuery programs and inline Articraft geometry routines while preserving URDF articulation specifications. Each program is paired with its associated assets, textual descriptions, provenance, and available verification signals. We further develop 3DCodeVerse Harness, 3D code generation harness for synthesizing and refining complex 3D programs from text, images, or videos. The harness decomposes multi-component projects into directed acyclic graph (DAG) of coding and assembly tasks, allowing multiple agents to develop and integrate source files in structured manner. Generated programs are executed and rendered, after which an independent judge agent evaluates the outputs against explicit acceptance criteria. Complementary spatial checks detect structural inconsistencies and prevent visually plausible but geometrically invalid solutions from receiving high scores. The resulting feedback is then converted into localized repair objectives, enabling repeated executionevaluationrevision cycles 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code without human intervention. Through this iterative process, the harness supports inference-time scaling to complex projects containing thousands of lines of code. Importantly, 3DCodeVerse Harness serves not only as an inference system but also as datageneration engine. By recording successful programs, failed attempts, targeted repairs, and preference comparisons, its execution traces provide supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and preference learning. Together, 3DCodeVerse-2M and 3DCodeVerse Harness establish not only reusable infrastructure for 3D coding, but also closed loop connecting data construction, program synthesis, verification, refinement, and model improvement. We further support this ecosystem with open models and reproducible training recipes. Fine-tuning on 3DCodeVerse-2M substantially improves executable 3D code generation, reaching execution rates of 84.9% with 9B model and 92.9% with 27B model on 3DCodeBench. Moreover, 3DCodeVerse Harness consistently improves generation quality across coding agents, yielding gains of 15.529.1 points over one-shot generation.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Datasets and Benchmarks for 3D Coding. Learning to generate 3D content as code benefits from supervision over its construction procedures. DeepCAD and Fusion 360 Gallery expose CAD construction sequences, and Text2CAD connects such sequences to natural language (Wu et al., 2021; Willis et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2024). This supervision has expanded to executable CadQuery and Blender programs for reconstruction and language-conditioned generation through BlendNet, CADRecode, CAD-Coder, and MeshCoder (Du et al., 2024; Rukhovich et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026). Complementary procedural resources broaden the content represented by code: Infinigen and its extensions generate assets and scenes (Raistrick et al., 2023; 2024; Joshi et al., 2025), while Shaders21k provides programs for procedural image synthesis (Baradad et al., 2022). Existing benchmarks assess the resulting code generation, editing, and physics capabilities (Alrashedy et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026b; Shen et al., 2026). However, our paper focuses on scaling executable supervision across these heterogeneous coding environments. Our 3DCodeVerse-2M provides million-scale training corpus spanning CAD, Blender, shaders, and browser graphics, with programs that are self-contained within their respective target runtimes. Its construction combines curated existing sources with automated program generation and execution-based filtering, enabling continued data expansion for training open 3D coding models. Harness Engineering for 3D Coding. Execution and feedback allow 3D coding agents to inspect and revise the content produced by their programs. Systems such as 3D-GPT, SceneCraft, and LL3M establish language-driven planning and program generation for 3D modeling (Sun et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025). Executing and rendering these programs enables visual refinement, as explored by BlenderAlchemy, CADCodeVerify, and VIGA (Huang et al., 2024; Alrashedy et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026). Beyond rendered appearance, Articraft provides structured asset validation through specialized SDK, while Bioinspired123D connects script quality control with graph-based agentic workflow (Luu & Buehler, 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026). 3DHarnessBench further studies how the observation and tool interfaces available to an agent affect 3D reconstruction (Liu et al., 2026). In contrast, our 3DCodeVerse harness provides reusable execution and verification framework across coding backends, jointly supporting inference-time refinement and scalable training data curation. Its multi-agent directed acyclic graph coordinates execution, rendering, spatial measurements, and structural checks across static and articulated objects, scenes, and visual effects. sections.title: 5.1 RESULTS OF 3DCODEVERSE HARNESS
sections.content: Evaluation setup. We compare 3DCodeVerse against models with their native harnesses and Claude Design on 100 text-to-3D object prompts. We further compare against native harnesses on articulatedobject generation, 50 scene prompts, and 50 graphics prompts. We evaluate generation quality using three metrics. Human Preference is the fraction of anonymized side-by-side comparisons won according to human evaluators, with ties split equally. VLM Preference is the fraction of the same comparisons won according to VLM judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro), with ties split equally. Judge Score is Gemini 3.1 Pros overall rubric score, combining weighted criteria with defect penalties and score caps (0100; failed generations receive score of zero). Following 3DCodeBench (Gao et al., 2026b), we additionally report SigLIP-2 (Tschannen et al., 2025) textimage cosine similarity averaged over four views. The evaluation judge is described in Appendix C.3, and further evaluation details are in Appendix C.3. Main Results. Figure 4 shows consistent pattern across backbones and tasks: outputs from the native harness are rarely preferred, while the same backbone within 3DCodeVerse Harness wins most comparisons. On 3D objects, Human Preference for 3DCodeVerse Harness ranges from 69% to 89%, while Judge Score improves by 1125 points. The largest gains occur for the weaker models, including Gemini 3.8 Flash (61 to 87) and GPT-6 Luna (64 to 86). Against Claude Design, which uses Claude Opus 5.5, 3DCodeVerse Harness with the same backbone is preferred in 90% of human comparisons and achieves Judge Score of 88 versus 37. The same pattern extends to articulated objects, scenes, and graphics, where Human Preference reaches 7888%. The agreement between human preference and rubric-based scores suggests that the gains are not specific to the VLM rubric used during refinement. 6 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Figure 4: Main results of 3DCodeVerse Harness across four 3D coding tasks. Panels show (a) 3D objects, (b) articulated objects, (c) scenes, and (d) graphics. Blue bars report Human Preference (%), and orange bars report Judge Score (0100; failed generations receive score of zero). Hatched bars denote each backbones native harness, while solid bars denote 3DCodeVerse Harness. The final group in (a) compares Claude Design with 3DCodeVerse Harness, both using Claude Opus 5.5.

sections.title: 6 APPLICATIONS OF 3D CODING
sections.content: Robotics. 3D coding enables the construction of articulated assets and scenes with explicit geometry and physical constraints for simulated robot tasks. Programs encode rigid-link geometry, joint axes, and joint limits as editable parameters, supporting programmatic checks and controlled variation of object dimensions, articulation, and initial poses. These task instances can be executed in simulations to generate robot interactions and observations. To provide preliminary evaluation, we import an articulated asset validated and exported with 3DCodeVerse tools into MuJoCo and compare rendered observations with frozen UWM (Zhu et al., 2025) predictions across 12 cases spanning two assets, two contact states, and three control sequences, using complete scene state for rendering and image history with matched robot commands for UWM. Code renders and their UWM VAE reconstructions each pass fixed door-and-handle geometry check in 12/12 outputs, versus 7/36 UWM predictions. These results show that 3D code can help generate articulated assets and scenes for robotics simulation with explicit geometry and physical constraints. Video generation. 3D coding provides an editable interface for controlling the spatial and temporal conditions of video generation. Programs specify scene layout, object articulation and motion, and camera trajectories. We render generated 3D scenes using programs and harness them as reference videos, using the full sequences to condition Gemini Omni Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026) and Seedance 2.5 (ByteDance Seed, 2026). The rendered videos supply spatial and temporal guidance, while the video models are used to refine visual appearance. We present paired reference and generated frames to examine how the specified layout, object motion, and camera trajectories are preserved. This application connects explicit scene programs with video synthesis.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we present 3DCodeVerse, an open ecosystem that provides shared foundation for 3D coding through datasets, reusable harness, and open model baselines. The dataset brings together programs across coding environments with descriptions, associated assets, and available quality records. The harness combines execution, spatial checks, and visual judgment to support iterative generation without human feedback during run, while retaining the resulting programs and revisions for data curation. Experiments demonstrate the utility of the data for training open models and the benefits of the harness for existing coding agents. We will release the datasets, harness, models, and training recipes to support further research on 3D generation through code. 9 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code

THE 3DCODEVERSE HARNESS: DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION A.1 COMPONENTS AND MODEL ROLES Tracks and runtimes. 3DCodeVerse Harness spans four generative tracksstatic objects, articulated objects, 3D scenes, and procedural graphicsbacked by seven isolated language runtimes: three for static objects (Blender Python, CadQuery, and Three.js), one each for articulated mechanisms (URDF with Blender-authored links) and scenes (Three.js), and two for graphics (GLSL and moderngl). Each runtime specifies strict file layout, static lint rules, sandboxed build wrapper, canonical export formats, and deterministic render driver, while sharing unified coordinate frames, metric units, camera rigs, and geometric tolerances. Model roles and execution invariants. Each run decouples structural planning, code synthesis, and visual evaluation into three pluggable roles: planner, coding agent, and visionlanguage judge (Figure 7). The planner and judge operate through unified API interface, while the coding agent executes inside an isolated workspace equipped with the harnesss spatial tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), alongside single-shot mode that requests complete file envelope through direct API calls. Every round commits raw source code from which meshes and renders are deterministically regenerated; boilerplate infrastructure (camera rigging, coordinate conversion, URDF composition, scene assembly, and shader headers) resides in the harness, and verification proceeds strictly from fast programmatic gates to blind VLM judging. A.2 PLANNING AND THE JOB GRAPH Structured specification and plan synthesis. The planner translates an open-ended request into schema-validated structural plan: named parts with metric bounding boxes, materials, symmetry, and attachment topology for static objects; kinematic tree with typed joints, axes, pivots, limits, and acyclic affine mimic couplings (qj = mjqi + bj) for articulated mechanisms; spatial zones, modular assets, effects, and authored cameras for scenes; and render passes, uniforms, and temporal dynamics for graphics. Each plan carries an acceptance checklist binding items to an evidence modality (measurement, visual inspection, probe, or joint sweep) and priority (must or should), supplemented by canonical rules that normalize kinematic conventions and enforce requested dimensions (5%), triangle budgets, grounding, and temporal motion. 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Figure 8: From structural plan to file scopes and coding sessions, illustrated on the recorded trajectory of A.6. The planner decomposes the prompt into named parts with metric bounding boxes, materials, attachment relations, and an acceptance checklist; each target maps to its owned source files, and refinement tasks sharing files are grouped into file-disjoint sessions. In Round 1, nine revision tasks partition into eight file-disjoint groups; in Round 2, four tasks form four groups. Bounded plan verification. Planning executes as structured-output call with token budget scaled to the target part count. Range or formatting violations are repaired in-context, whereas degenerate kinematic hierarchy referencing undeclared links triggers clean context reset from the original request (C.5). File-scoped subtree decomposition. Each runtime maps plan targets to strict file-ownership scopes (per-part modules plus an assembly entry file for Blender and Three.js objects; single program for CadQuery, URDF, and graphics; and per-zone and per-asset modules for scenes), and writes outside sessions scope are reverted between Git commits. Objects with eight or more top-level parts in modular languages are synthesized via scoped sessions over attachment subtrees of at most three partseach supplied with the planned bounding boxes of adjacent partsfollowed by an assembly session (Figure 8). During refinement, tasks that share files are grouped into connected components and dispatched as file-disjoint sessions, bounding per-session context and preventing cross-part regressions (C.5), while best-of-N candidates and scene assets run concurrently in isolated workspaces. Session context and contract injection. Every agent workspace is provisioned with standardized instruction specification containing the runtime invariants, track-specific tool schemas, and language contracts. Each task prompt supplies the user request, coordinate-frame conventions, the language cookbook, the structural plan formatted as exact metric tables with its acceptance checklist, and the verification protocol (requiring clean build followed by spatial measurement or probing). Single-shot prompts inline the code skeleton and request complete file envelope in single response. A.3 SPATIAL TOOLS AND DETERMINISTIC GATES Semantic verdicts vs. transport errors. Every tool response separates the semantic verification verdict (PASS/FAIL) from the tool execution status. detected mesh collision or build failure is returned as valid observation leading with structured FAIL verdict; only an internal tool crash sets the MCP protocol error flag, preventing commercial coding agents from entering degenerate transport-retry loops (C.5). Tool responses bound text length and image resolution, attaching diagnostic renders specifically when check identifies actionable geometric defects. Deterministic gates, connectivity, and plan adherence. Following each successful build, the track pipeline executes its deterministic gates. Gate errors compile into high-priority revision tasks with numerical fix hints and impose hard upper bounds on the rounds rubric score, while warnings are 16 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Figure 9: Observations, deterministic gates, and authoring-frame feedback. measured geometric defect is returned as structured negative verdict rather than protocol error (left); single verification routine serves simultaneously as an interactive agent tool, an end-of-round gate, and generator of prioritized revision tasks (middle). Right: baseline-round diagnostics from A.6, with corrective translation vectors projected directly into the agents native authoring frame. surfaced to the judge. Conversely, passing deterministic gate vetoes contradictory visual defect claims from the VLM judge (A.4). In the connectivity gate, the ground-contacting component with the largest face count defines the primary support structure, and any disconnected component is reported alongside its nearest supported neighbour and the exact 3D translation vector that closes the gap. contact ledger tracks all planned part attachments with their measured clearances while enforcing structural support at the global assembly level. The contract gate verifies built part counts, orientations, and bounding-box extents against the structural plan within per-axis tolerances. Authoring-frame diagnostic projection. Although exported meshes are evaluated in the canonical Y-up frame, all corrective fix hints are projected back into each runtimes native authoring frame: seat floating by 12 mm receives corrective translation of (0, 0, 0.012) in Z-up Blender Python and (0, 0.012, 0) in Y-up Three.js (Figure 9). Articulated diagnostics output URDF joint origins and axes directly, and scene diagnostics emit native scene-graph API instructions. A.4 AUTOMATED JUDGMENT Evidence payload and response schema. single payload builder serves in-loop refinement, post-run evaluation, and judge calibration (Figure 10). The judge receives the request, plan digest, acceptance checklist, measurements, gate findings, and track telemetry, together with up to five labelled multi-view montages, detail crops, andwhen connectivity errors occurcross-sectional slices, with montage order randomized per sample to remove positional bias. On object tracks, passing connectivity gate prohibits unverified visual claims of floating or interpenetrating parts. The judge answers in strict JSON schema at temperature 0.2, stating its evidence, strengths, issues, defect votes, and checklist verifications before assigning criterion scores and up to six prioritized improvement instructions; deterministic criteria such as silhouette IoU are injected by code. Score aggregation and deterministic vetoing. For round t, sample scores for each rubric criterion are averaged into s(t) , while checklist verifications and binary defects are aggregated by majority vote. Any VLM-voted structural defect is automatically vetoedincurring neither penalty nor capwhenever the corresponding deterministic gate executed, passed without error, and recorded no penetration warning of 8 mm or deeper. The judge inspects structured telemetry and labelled multi-view montages without access to source code or generator reasoning (left); its schema enforces explicit visual observation prior to criterion scoring (middle). Right: baseline-round score computation for A.6, combining criterion means, majority-voted defects, and deterministic gate caps. where ˆd(t) {0, 1} denotes retained defects with penalty weights λd, and u(t) [0, 1] is the tightest upper bound among retained defect caps, triggered gate caps, and unverified mandatory checklist items (u(t) = 1 when none apply; on object tracks, verifying of mandatory items sets the checklist cap to 0.6 + 0.4 v/m). round achieves pass verdict when s(t) meets the track threshold, every criterion exceeds its floor, and all mandatory items are verified. Every applied cap and its triggering evidence are archived in the verdict record. Pairwise comparison and judge repeatability. For pairwise preference evaluation, the judge inspects anonymized candidates under both display orders and declares winner only when both orders concur; reference-conditioned and likeness modes additionally incorporate measured silhouette IoU and real-world photographs. Across repeated evaluations of fixed chair and cabinet artifacts under shuffled montage orders, Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves mean score standard deviation of 0.030 (0.035 under fixed order, compared with 0.083 for Gemini 3.8 Flash), confirming that our primary evaluator provides high-precision, view-order-robust scoring signal (C.3). A.5 REFINEMENT ROUNDS, HISTORY, AND OUTPUT SELECTION Round execution and task prioritization. Pre-round stages are cached, whereas every round executes fresh through fixed verification chain: code synthesis, build with bounded repair, geometric measurement, deterministic gates, multi-view rendering, VLM judgment, and Git archival. failed build triggers up to three targeted repair sessions supplied with the error location, traceback, lint diagnostics, and relevant cookbook snippets, and every completed round is committed with journal entry of its telemetry, verdicts, renders, and token usage. Refinement tasks are compiled from the preceding round in strict priority orderdeterministic gate errors with numerical fix hints, then unverified mandatory checklist items, then the judges perceptual instructionsand deduplicated by part and defect category. At most six tasks are dispatched per round, and truncation applies only to perceptual suggestions, so gate errors and mandatory items are never dropped; reference-conditioned runs append silhouette task whenever outline IoU falls below 0.60. Termination and best-of-N initialization. The standard profile allocates up to = 4 refinement rounds and 60-minute wall-clock ceiling; refinement stops early once all verification tasks are resolved, round makes no code change, or the budget is reached, while monetary cost is logged for accounting only. With multi-candidate initialization, the baseline round synthesizes independent 18 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Figure 11: Recorded trajectory for the prompt three-legged wooden stool on the Three.js runtime under the economy profile. Each column shows one round: the rendered view inspected by the judge, the composite score with its penalties and caps, deterministic gate findings, and VLM defect votes. Closed-loop refinement resolves all baseline floating and interpenetrating parts in Round 1 (0.410 0.844) and refines geometric detailing in Round 2 (11,052 triangles, reaching 0.933 under the strict metric-footprint cap), completing in 4.0 active minutes at $0.74. candidates, ranks them lexicographically by build success, quick rubric score, and gate error count on four-view rig, and seeds Round 0 with the winner. Post-run output selection. Judged rounds are ranked by composite rubric score, breaking ties by fewer gate errors and earlier round index. When the top two rounds fall within 0.03, an optional pairwise VLM tie-breaker promotes the runner-up only if it wins both presentation orders with confidence 0.60. The selected round is packaged directly from its Git commit and verified artifacts without re-executing the build. A.6 RECORDED RUN Figure 11 traces complete run for the prompt three-legged wooden stool on the Three.js runtime under the economy profile. The planner decomposes the stool into seven parts (a circular seat slab, three splayed legs, and three through-tenon wedges) with eleven checklist items, including In the baseline round (t = 0), the initial script builds, but four signature structural features. deterministic gates identify multiple structural violations: the connectivity gate detects three wedge seat interpenetrations ( 22 mm) and six disconnected parts floating up to 212 mm from the support component; two legs exceed their planned bounding-box tolerances; and the mesh contains only 1,572 triangles against detail floor of 2,450, yielding composite score of 0.410 (0.59 weighted criterion mean minus 0.18 in defect penalties). The harness compiles nine prioritized revision tasks eight from deterministic gate errors with exact authoring-frame translation vectors and one from the footprint specificationand dispatches them across eight file-disjoint sessions. By Round 1, every structural defect is resolved: all seven parts form single ground-supported assembly with nine verified contacts, lifting the score by +0.434 to 0.844. Round 2 addresses the remaining geometric and metric refinementscarving recessed mortise slots, chamfering the slab rims, and increasing leg splayexpanding mesh detail to 11,052 triangles and reaching score of 0.933 (bounded by the graded checklist cap of 0.6 + 0.4 5/6 for 0.34 vs. 0.38 base diameter). Link geometry is authored in Blender and kinematic structure in URDF; the build verifies rest-pose frame agreement, and the joint sweep articulates the mechanism across its motion limits. The dynamic sweep automatically detects subtle 2.5 mm hingebase collision at the upper opening limit that is invisible at rest, enforcing physical articulability via the rubric cap. A.7 ARTICULATED OBJECTS: GEOMETRY, KINEMATICS, AND JOINT SWEEPS The articulated track coordinates two coupled source representations (Figure 12): Blender Python script authoring one mesh per link in world coordinates at the rest pose, and URDF specification placing each link frame at its kinematic pivot. A.8 SCENES AND GRAPHICS Scenes. Scene synthesis executes staged hierarchical pipeline prior to the main refinement loop (Figure 13a). Individual scene assets (up to eight, or four under tight budget thresholds) follow progressive compute-escalation policy: each asset begins with fast single-shot draft and deterministic check, escalating to full interactive agent session only if automated repair does not resolve all findings; Blender-built hero assets additionally undergo VLM evaluation with monotonic quality gate that retains revision pass only if it strictly improves the asset score. Environmental terrains and spatial zone layouts are built concurrently, followed by unified cross-zone composition session and deterministic scene-graph assembly. To guarantee timely completion on complex prompts, pre-round staging is bounded at 55% of the wall-clock budget, dynamically switching remaining pre-round stages to fast single-shot synthesis once reached. Scene gates enforce asset grounding and 20 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Figure 13: Scene and procedural graphics tracks. (a) Scene generation executes staged asset-andzone assembly pipeline before entering the closed-loop refinement cycle with scene-specific gates. (b) Graphics generation synthesizes fragment shaders or OpenGL programs whose temporal frames are sampled at fixed timestamps, verified by statistical frame gates, and evaluated as multi-frame montages. collision bounds, runtime console cleanliness, per-camera exposure and framing coverage, inter-frame animation motion, asset utilization, and 15,000 draw-call budget across up to ten authored and overview camera views. Graphics. On the graphics track, the agent authors either Shadertoy-style GLSL fragment shader (with optional multipass feedback buffers) or moderngl Python program defining setup and per-frame render routines, while the harness injects standardized headers, uniforms, outputs, and brief-matched reference recipes (Figure 13b). Sequences are rendered at {0, 1, 2.5, 4, 6} (clipped to the loop duration) at 1280 720 resolution. The deterministic frame gate measures luminance distribution, colourfulness, edge density, inter-frame motion, and pixel validity: NaN, all-black, or overexposed frames trigger hard errors, while static or flickering sequences trigger score-capping warnings. The judge evaluates multi-frame montages paired with frame telemetry, and each refinement round dispatches unified whole-program optimization task. The catalogue indexes 269,597 unique executable programs across nine collections  (Table 5)  , spanning parametric CAD, procedural Blender Python, OpenSCAD, articulated URDF mechanisms, Three.js scenes, and GLSL shaders. The benchmark training pairs (768,596 pairs, 891 tokens) are deduplicated promptcode splits, including web-animation programs, built for the fine-tuning experiments of 5.2 and Appendix C.1; they strictly exclude all 3DCodeBench procedural factories, seeded instances, and per-dialect evaluation suites. The unified text export (2,028,286 rows across 342 shards) expands each curated program across its three caption views (visual description, instruction, and factory recipe) and decomposes multi-pass shaders into pass-level targets: 891,788 native-format rows, 848,819 standardized text-export rows, and 287,679 pass-flattened shader rows. B.2 SOURCES AND CONVERSION PIPELINES DeepCAD to CadQuery. DeepCAD provides 178,238 raw sketchextrusion command sequences rather than executable programs (Wu et al., 2021). Our deterministic compiler translates each command sequence into self-contained CadQuery script: 174,981 sequences compile (98.2%), 174,177 produce valid watertight solids (97.7%), and vector-level hashing removes 25.8% exact geometric duplicates to yield 128,201 unique executable programs (71.9% of raw sequences). Geometric fidelity against the original solids, measured via voxel IoU at 483 resolution, averages 0.985, with 96.9% of programs exceeding 0.90 (the remaining 1,114 programs are annotated with explicit fidelity metadata so downstream pipelines can apply custom thresholds). Natural-language annotations from Text2CAD (Khan et al., 2024) are paired with 125,162 programs under their original license terms, accompanied by four canonical views per solid. sections.content: C.1 TRAINING DETAILS Training configuration. All fine-tuning runs are conducted with LLaMA-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024) on 4 NVIDIA H100 (80 GB) GPUs in bfloat16 precision using gradient checkpointing and sequence packing. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) applies LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) of rank 64 (α = 128, dropout 0.05) across all linear projections with learning rate of 1 104 (or 1 105 for full-parameter fine-tuning under ZeRO-3 (Rajbhandari et al., 2020)), cosine learning-rate schedule, 5% linear warm-up ratio, and per-device batch size of 1 with gradient accumulation of 8 (4 for 27B). Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al. 2023) initializes from the merged SFT checkpoint and trains rank-16 LoRA (α = 32) for 2 epochs under sigmoid preference loss (β = 0.1, learning rate 5 106). The sequence context length is set to 8,192 tokens for 9B runs and 4,096 tokens for 27B runs to fit single-device memory bounds under data-parallel training. Evaluation 23 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code inference uses vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) under greedy decoding or temperature sampling (T =0.7) as specified per experiment. Training throughput. Because LoRA introduces compact optimizer state, training the 27B model under standard Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) avoids ZeRO-3 parameter all-gather traffic and achieves 13 higher step throughput (6.2 vs. 460 tokens/s) with standard PyTorch allocator caching. Across 4 H100 GPUs, 9B LoRA sustains 17 tokens/s (completing the 270 K-pair, 293 M-token mixture in 4 46 m), while 27B LoRA sustains 6.2 tokens/s. Chat formatting and strict contamination control. Training examples are formatted as ShareGPT multi-turn conversations: system prompt specifying the target dialect and output contract, user turn containing the natural-language specification, and an assistant turn containing the complete executable program in fenced code block. Any example whose tokenized conversation exceeds the context window is excluded cleanly rather than truncated, preserving syntactic closure. To guarantee zero traintest leakage, all 212 3DCodeBench procedural factories, all 3,904 re-seeded instances derived from those factories, and all per-dialect evaluation splits are strictly held out; no training mixture shares program or asset identifier with any evaluation task. Three LoRA runs share an identical optimization recipe and vary solely in which representation views of the unified text export (Appendix B.1) they consume. Optimization recipe. Each run applies LoRA of rank 16 (α = 32, dropout 0.05) for one epoch at peak learning rate of 5 105 with linear warm-up over the first 3% of steps and cosine decay to zero. Examples are packed into full sequences (7.2 samples per sequence), with each optimizer step consuming 64 packed sequences and logging training cross-entropy every five steps. Representation scaling arms. Arm trains on the complete unified export across all three representation views (native format, standardized text export, and pass-flattened multi-pass shaders): 1,992,816 rows packed into 276,594 sequences (4,322 steps). Arm trains on the native-format and pass-flattened views without the re-templated text-export variant: 1,160,630 rows in 159,427 sequences (2,492 steps). Arm retains single canonical copy of each curated program paired with its instruction-style caption: 292,690 rows in 39,926 sequences (647 steps). Optimization dynamics across representation scales. Figure 14 demonstrates smooth, stable convergence across all three regimes: no logged step exceeds 1.3 the trailing 20-step moving average, and all runs are entirely free of instability or divergence spikes. Rapid initial adaptation occurs within the first quarter of the epochreducing cross-entropy from 0.60 to 0.30 (Arm A) and 0.36 (Arms and C)followed by steady refinement to terminal smoothed losses of 0.274 (Arm A), 0.314 (Arm B), and 0.292 (Arm C), with Arm stabilizing across the second half of the epoch (0.277 at mid-epoch to 0.274 at completion). C.3 EVALUATION PROTOCOL Code extraction and geometric evaluation for open models. For open-model evaluations (5.2), generated responses pass through deterministic code extractor that strips reasoning blocks, collects fenced code blocks (including trailing unterminated blocks), and ranks candidates by dialect markers, fence annotations, and AST syntactic validity. This extraction step is essential for pretrained reasoning checkpoints: with thinking enabled, 52 of 212 responses from the zero-shot 27B model omit markdown fences and 74 place auxiliary snippets after the main program, whereas fine-tuned models adhere strictly to the single-block output contract (100% single-fence compliance). Extracted programs execute inside the dialects pinned runtime under 300 timeout. Resulting meshes are exported to GLB, centred at the origin, normalized to unit maximum extent, uniformly sampled at 10,000 surface points, and evaluated via symmetric Chamfer-L2 distance and F-score at thresholds τ {0.05, 0.10} (taking the best alignment across the four 90 yaw rotations; ground-truth reference scripts self-verify at Chamfer 0.016 and F@0.05 1.0). Object prompts and compared systems. The 3D object benchmark comprises 100 Three.js generation prompts stratified across three specification levels21 concise (simple), 17 moderate (medium), and 62 richly specified (detailed) promptstesting synthesis across varying levels of structural and stylistic complexity without prescribing explicit metric dimensions or part lists. All systems are evaluated under uniform single-request deliverable protocol: each workflow receives the identical user prompt string and delivers final executable program, which is rebuilt and scored by our common evaluator. For commercial product baselines such as Claude Design (powered by Claude Opus 5.5), we evaluate its released reference outputs directly in our unified evaluation pipeline without modification. We evaluate Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Opus 5.5 against their respective native baselines on the primary 60-prompt benchmark, and evaluate Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra on balanced 30-prompt subset (10 prompts per specification level). Each native baseline  (Table 14)  synthesizes code in single pass using its standard coding-agent backend (high reasoning effort for Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5; medium effort for GPT-6 Astra; direct API for Gemini 3.8 Flash), whereas 3DCodeVerse Harness wraps the identical backbone model with structured planning, spatial tools, and automated verification. This paired design directly isolates the end-to-end gain of the 3DCodeVerse Harness workflow for fixed backbone model, with token telemetry and API-equivalent cost reported alongside quality metrics  (Table 8)  . 25 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Single-request autonomy and refinement horizons. The single-request protocol prohibits humanin-the-loop intervention: each system receives one user prompt with zero subsequent human edits or manual candidate cherry-picking, while permitting autonomous internal tool calls and verification passes. Our primary object benchmark evaluates single-round harness execution (T = 0 in the notation of 4), retaining the initial planned generation, interactive tool use, automated build repair, and final verification (using Gemini 3.8 Flash as planner and Gemini 3.1 Pro as in-loop judge for the Flash runs). Multi-round studies (T = 4) extend this autonomous loop with up to four closed-loop refinement rounds and automated post-run output selection under the same single user request. Independent evaluation judge. All Judge Scores and VLM Preferences reported in 5 are produced by single frozen evaluation pipeline that applies the judgment architecture and track rubrics of Appendix A.4 independently of the generation workflow under test. Each delivered program is rebuilt from scratch in its pinned runtime, with failed builds scored zero, to extract geometric measurements, connectivity or kinematic-sweep telemetry, and canonical multi-view renders (fourteen shaded views plus clay views for objects, multi-pose sweeps for articulated mechanisms, authored and orbital views at two timestamps for scenes, and sampled frame sheets for graphics); Gemini 3.1 Pro then scores it three times. Three safeguards decouple evaluation from in-loop refinement: (1) clean-room rebuild and blind prompting, scoring every artifact against the raw user prompt and prompt-derived checklist alone, with all harness-generated plans, internal checklists, and refinement histories stripped; (2) deterministic geometric caps, bounding scores via exact mesh connectivity and kinematic checks independent of VLM perception (Eq. 5); and (3) multi-metric validation, pairing Judge Scores with SigLIP-2 similarity and blind human pairwise preferences (5), which consistently corroborate the rubric gains across all four tracks. Visual-criterion ablation. Our primary metric, the overall Judge Score Sall  (Table 14)  , combines seven weighted object criteriaintent fidelity (0.22), structural plausibility (0.18), geometry detail (0.16), proportions and scale (0.12), assembly fit (0.12), materials (0.10), and craftsmanship (0.10) with deterministic defect penalties and caps (Eq. 5). To verify that our gains over external baselines such as Claude Design do not stem merely from metric-scale conventions or hard structural caps on open-ended prompts, we additionally compute an uncapped, scale-free visual score in Tables 7 and 9: Svis = (cid:80) k=scale wksk (cid:80) k=scale wk , (7) which aggregates raw criterion means sk prior to aggregate defect penalties and score caps while excluding the proportions-and-scale criterion (with failed builds scored zero on both metrics). Even under this forgiving, uncapped metric, 3DCodeVerse Harness outperforms Claude Design by +25.6 points (88.1 vs. 62.4, winning 58 of 60 prompts), confirming that its advantage reflects superior geometric fidelity and visual craftsmanship rather than rubric thresholding. sections.title: D EXECUTABLE ARTICULATION AND COMPARISON WITH UWM
sections.content: Explicit kinematic simulation vs. latent video rollouts. Complementing the robotics application in 6, we examine how executable 3D code preserves rigid-link structure during robot manipulation compared with frozen video world-action model, UWM (Zhu et al., 2025). Using an articulated microwave asset synthesized by GPT-6 Astra and verified by 3DCodeVerse Harness tooling (passing forward-kinematics, rigid-distance, and hinge-sweep gates across five poses), we instantiate MuJoCo simulation alongside the native reference asset across two initial contact states and three robot control sequencescontact push, hold, and retreatyielding 12 evaluation cases. Each rollout executes 16 matched robot action commands at 20 Hz: UWM generates three seeded video rollouts per case (36 total) from observation history and action commands, whereas code simulation steps the explicit articulated asset directly inside MuJoCo. Quantitative evaluation of structural preservation. To measure whether rollouts maintain coherent rigid-part geometry under physical interaction, we apply calibrated orientation-aware doorand-handle contour detector across all outputs. Calibrated prior to evaluation on 24 held-out static renders across six hinge angles and four robot poses, the detector recovers the true hinge angle within 1 on all 20 accepted detections and abstains whenever contours degrade or become ambiguous. To isolate latent dynamics drift from autoencoder reconstruction blur, we additionally evaluate VAE-reconstructed code control by passing every simulator render through UWMs frozen VAE encoder and decoder. Across all 72 evaluated outputs  (Table 18)  , both direct code simulation and VAE-reconstructed code renders satisfy the geometric criterion in 12/12 (100%) rollouts, whereas UWM predictions satisfy the criterion in only 7/36 (19.4%) rollouts (29/36 fail to preserve assessable door-and-handle contours). Complementary strengths of simulator-ready 3D code. Table 18 and Figures 1516 clarify the structural advantage of programmatic 3D assets for embodied simulation. While static last-frame baseline trivially preserves initial contours (12/12) by predicting zero motion, pixel-space world models synthesize motion directly in latent space at the cost of frequent contour distortion across random seeds. By contrast, compiling generated 3D code into physics simulator combines both properties: the simulator enforces exact rigid-body transformations, joint axes, and articulated state transitions over time while maintaining crisp, view-consistent geometry across contact push, hold, and retreat controls. 33 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Figure 16: Articulated code simulation vs. UWM rollouts on the generated asset (Initial State 2).
